Telecom Customer Churn - Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Churn is when a paying customer cancels the service. It matters commercially because acquiring a replacement customer costs several times more than keeping an existing one, so a churn rate is really a measure of how much the business must spend just to stand still.

In this dataset 26.5% of customers have churned - roughly one in four. That is high enough that the interesting question is not "do we have a churn problem?" but "which customers churn, and what do they have in common?"

This notebook works through that question in order:

  1. Setup and load - get the data in.
  2. Describe - what every column means.
  3. Clean - fix the one broken column and explain the missing values rather than silently deleting them.
  4. Profile the target - establish the 26.5% baseline that every later chart is read against.
  5. Univariate analysis - the shape of each variable on its own.
  6. Bivariate analysis - churn rate for every customer attribute. This is the core.
  7. Multivariate analysis - how the strongest drivers combine.
  8. Findings and recommendations - what the business should actually do.

How to read every chart in this notebook¶

Most churn analyses plot counts of churned customers, and that is misleading: the largest group will always contain the most churners simply because it is the largest. So nearly every chart here plots the churn rate within each group instead, with the group size n under each bar and a dashed line at the overall 26.5% baseline.

Above the dashed line = a risk segment (red). Below it = a safe segment (blue).

1. Setup¶

All imports live in this one cell so the notebook runs top-to-bottom from a fresh kernel.

In [73]:
# Data handling
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# Visualisation
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)
pd.set_option("display.width", 120)

# --- Chart theme ---------------------------------------------------------
# The built-in "ggplot" theme supplies the whole look: grey panel, white grid,
# and its own colour cycle. The only thing we take from it by hand are the first
# two cycle colours, so the risk/safe rule stays the same on every chart.
plt.style.use("ggplot")

RISK, SAFE = plt.rcParams["axes.prop_cycle"].by_key()["color"][:2]   # red, blue

print("Libraries loaded. pandas", pd.__version__, "| numpy", np.__version__)
print("ggplot theme applied - risk =", RISK, "| safe =", SAFE)

Two things stand out already:

  • 7,043 customers and 21 columns - a comfortable size for analysis.
  • TotalCharges is stored as object (text), not a number, even though it is clearly money. That is a data-quality problem, and we fix it in section 4.

3. What the columns mean¶

# Column Name Description
1 customerID The unique ID of each customer
2 Gender The gender of a person
3 SeniorCitizen Whether a customer can be classified as a senior citizen (1 = yes, 0 = no).
4 Partner If a customer is married / in a live-in relationship.
5 Dependents If a customer has dependents (children / retired parents).
6 Tenure The time in months for which a customer has been using the service.
7 PhoneService Whether a customer has a landline phone service along with the internet service.
8 MultipleLines Whether a customer has multiple lines of connectivity.
9 InternetService The type of internet service chosen by the customer.
10 OnlineSecurity Specifies if a customer has online security.
11 OnlineBackup Specifies if a customer has online backup.
12 DeviceProtection Specifies if a customer has opted for device protection.
13 TechSupport Whether a customer has opted for tech support or not.
14 StreamingTV Whether a customer has the option of TV streaming.
15 StreamingMovies Whether a customer has the option of movie streaming.
16 Contract The type of contract a customer has chosen.
17 PaperlessBilling Whether a customer has opted for paperless billing.
18 PaymentMethod Specifies the method by which bills are paid.
19 MonthlyCharges Specifies the money paid by a customer each month.
20 TotalCharges The total money paid by the customer to the company.
21 Churn The target variable - whether the customer has left.

The 20 non-target columns fall into three natural groups, and that is how sections 6 and 7 are organised:

  • Who the customer is - Gender, SeniorCitizen, Partner, Dependents
  • What they buy - PhoneService, MultipleLines, InternetService, and the six add-ons
  • How they pay - Contract, PaperlessBilling, PaymentMethod, MonthlyCharges, TotalCharges, Tenure

4. Data quality and cleaning¶

4.1 Fixing TotalCharges¶

TotalCharges arrived as text. Converting it with errors="coerce" turns anything that is not a valid number into NaN, which conveniently also counts the bad values for us.

In [77]:
df["TotalCharges"] = pd.to_numeric(df["TotalCharges"], errors="coerce")
print("Missing values after conversion:", df["TotalCharges"].isnull().sum())

Missing values after conversion: 11

4.2 Understanding the 11 missing values¶

Before deleting anything, it is worth asking which customers these are. A missing value that follows a pattern is telling us something; a missing value at random is just noise.

In [78]:
missing = df[df["TotalCharges"].isnull()]
print("Tenure values among rows with a missing TotalCharges:", missing["Tenure"].unique())
missing[["Tenure", "MonthlyCharges", "TotalCharges", "Contract", "Churn"]]

Tenure values among rows with a missing TotalCharges: [0]

6670 0 73.35 NaN Two year No

Every single one has Tenure == 0.

These are brand-new customers who signed up but have not been billed even once, so there is no total to record. The value is not missing at random - it is missing structurally, and the correct total for someone who has never been billed is 0.

So we fill with 0 rather than dropping the rows. Dropping would quietly discard 11 genuine, newly-acquired customers and would bias the very start of the tenure curve we plot in section 6.5. Note that all 11 are still active (Churn = No), which is exactly what you would expect of customers who joined this month.

5. The target variable: how many customers churn?¶

In [82]:

BASELINE = (df["Churn"] == "Yes").mean() * 100      # the reference line used everywhere

print(churn_counts.to_string())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))
bars = ax.bar(["Retained", "Churned"],
              [churn_counts["No"], churn_counts["Yes"]],
              width=0.5, color=[SAFE, RISK])
ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="%d", padding=3, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylabel("Customers")
ax.set_title("Churn is imbalanced: about 1 in 4 customers left")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Churn
No     5174
Yes    1869

Overall churn rate: 26.54%

Insight. 1,869 of 7,043 customers churned - 26.54%. Two consequences:

  1. This is our baseline. Any group churning noticeably above 26.5% is a risk segment; anything below it is a safe one. Every chart from here on draws it as a dashed line.
  2. The classes are imbalanced (roughly 3:1). Worth remembering if this data is later used for modelling - a model that simply predicted "nobody churns" would score 73% accuracy while being completely useless.

A reusable chart helper¶

Rather than rebuild the same pivot-and-plot code a dozen times, we define it once here. It draws the churn rate for each level of a column, labels each bar with that rate, puts the group size n in the tick label underneath, and draws the 26.5% baseline for comparison. Bars at or above the baseline are coloured red (risk), the rest blue (safe).

In [11]:
def churn_by_category(column, data=None, ax=None, title=None, order=None, labels=None):
    # Plot churn rate (%) per level of `column`, annotated with the group size n.
    data = df if data is None else data
    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 4))

    rate = data.groupby(column)["Churn"].apply(lambda s: (s == "Yes").mean() * 100)
    size = data[column].value_counts()
    if order is not None:
        rate, size = rate.reindex(order), size.reindex(order)
    size = size.reindex(rate.index)

    # Group size goes in the tick label, where it can never collide with a short bar.
    names = [labels.get(i, str(i)) for i in rate.index] if labels else [str(i) for i in rate.index]
    names = [f"{name}\n(n={n:,})" for name, n in zip(names, size.values)]

    colors = [RISK if v >= BASELINE else SAFE for v in rate.values]
    bars = ax.bar(names, rate.values, width=0.55, color=colors)
    ax.bar_label(bars, fmt="%.1f%%", padding=3, fontweight="bold", fontsize=9)

    ax.axhline(BASELINE, color="#555555", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2)
    ax.set_ylim(0, max(rate.max() * 1.28, BASELINE * 1.35))
    ax.set_ylabel("Churn rate (%)")
    ax.set_title(title or column)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
    return ax

print(f"Helper ready. Baseline churn rate = {BASELINE:.2f}% (the dashed line on every chart)")

Helper ready. Baseline churn rate = 26.54% (the dashed line on every chart)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4))

specs = [("Tenure",         "Months with the company", 36),
         ("MonthlyCharges", "Monthly bill ($)",        36),
         ("TotalCharges",   "Lifetime spend ($)",      36)]

for ax, (col, xlabel, bins) in zip(axes, specs):
    ax.hist(df[col], bins=bins, color=SAFE, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.6)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Customers")
    ax.set_title(col)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Insights from the three distributions.

  • Tenure is strongly bimodal - a tall spike at 1-2 months and another at 72 months, with a dip in the middle. The company either loses people almost immediately or keeps them for the full six years. There is not much of a "middle" customer. This single fact shapes the whole analysis: churn is a new-customer problem.
  • MonthlyCharges is also bimodal, clustering near $20 and again across $70-$100. The low cluster is phone-only customers; the high cluster is internet (especially fiber) bundles. So this column is really a proxy for which product a customer has.
  • TotalCharges is heavily right-skewed, which is expected because it is roughly tenure x monthly charge. Most customers have accumulated little; a long tail of loyal customers. Median $1,395 against a mean of \$2,280 confirms the skew.

Insight. The customer base is balanced on gender (3,555 male / 3,488 female) but skewed on almost everything else: only 16% are senior citizens, 55% are on a monthly contract, 59% use paperless billing, and 56% pay manually. Fiber optic is the single largest internet product (3,096 customers), and 1,526 customers take no internet at all. Those imbalances matter, because the largest groups are also - as the next section shows - the ones churning fastest.

7. Bivariate analysis - what drives churn¶

This is the heart analysis. For each attribute we ask a single question: does knowing this about a customer change how likely they are to leave?

Remember the reading rule: bars above the dashed 26.5% line are risk segments.

7.1 Demographics - who the customer is¶

In [29]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 8))

churn_by_category("Gender", ax=axes[0, 0], title="Gender")
churn_by_category("SeniorCitizen", ax=axes[0, 1], title="Senior citizen", order=[0, 1], labels={0: "Not senior", 1: "Senior"})
churn_by_category("Partner", ax=axes[1, 0], title="Has a partner")
churn_by_category("Dependents", ax=axes[1, 1], title="Has dependents")

fig.suptitle("Churn rate by demographic attribute (dashed line = 26.5% overall)",fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Insights.

  • Gender does not matter at all. 26.9% of women churn against 26.2% of men - a gap of 0.8 points, which is noise. This is worth stating plainly because gender is often the first thing people chart. It should not drive any retention decision.
  • Senior citizens churn at nearly double the rate of everyone else: 41.7% vs 23.6%. They are only 16% of the base, but they are one of its most fragile segments.
  • Customers with no partner (33.0%) and no dependents (31.3%) churn far more than those with a partner (19.7%) or dependents (15.5%).

Taken together, the last two points describe the same underlying customer: a single-person household. Family households behave like anchored, multi-user accounts - harder to switch away, and more people depending on the connection. Solo customers can leave suddenly.

7.2 Contract and billing - how the customer pays¶

In [16]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.5))

churn_by_category("Contract", ax=axes[0], title="Contract type",
                  order=["Monthly", "One year", "Two year"])
churn_by_category("PaperlessBilling", ax=axes[1], title="Paperless billing")
churn_by_category("PaymentMethod", ax=axes[2], title="Payment method",
                  order=["Manual", "Bank transfer (automatic)", "Credit card (automatic)"],
                  labels={"Bank transfer (automatic)": "Bank transfer\n(auto)",
                          "Credit card (automatic)": "Credit card\n(auto)"})

fig.suptitle("Churn rate by contract and billing (dashed line = 26.5% overall)",
             fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Insights - this is where the strongest signal in the whole dataset lives.

  • Contract type is the single biggest driver. Monthly contracts churn at 42.7%, one-year at 11.3%, two-year at just 2.8%. That is a 15x spread between the extremes, far wider than anything else we measure. And the worst group is also the largest: 3,875 customers - 55% of the base - are on monthly terms.
  • Paperless billing customers churn more than twice as often (33.6% vs 16.3%). This is almost certainly not the paper itself causing anything - paperless correlates with the newer, monthly, digitally-acquired customers. It is a useful marker of risk, not a lever.
  • Manual payment nearly doubles churn (34.7%) compared with either automatic method (16.7% bank transfer, 15.2% credit card). Every manual payment is a moment where the customer consciously decides to pay again; an automatic payment removes that decision.

A note on two year contract: a two-year contract does not magically create loyalty. It partly selects for customers who already intended to stay, and it also blocks the ones who want to leave. Both effects are real, and both are commercially useful.

7.3 Core services - what the customer buys¶

In [17]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.5))

churn_by_category("InternetService", ax=axes[0], title="Internet service",
                  order=["DSL", "Fiber optic", "No"],
                  labels={"No": "No internet"})
churn_by_category("PhoneService",  ax=axes[1], title="Phone service")
churn_by_category("MultipleLines", ax=axes[2], title="Multiple lines")

fig.suptitle("Churn rate by core service (dashed line = 26.5% overall)",
             fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Insights.

  • Fiber optic customers churn at 41.9% - more than double DSL's 19.0%, and they are the largest product group (3,096 customers). This is the most commercially interesting anomaly in the dataset: fiber is the premium, technically superior product, yet its customers leave fastest.
  • Customers with no internet churn at only 7.4% - by far the most loyal group. They are typically low-cost, phone-only, long-tenure customers with very little bill to resent.
  • Phone service is nearly irrelevant (26.7% with vs 24.9% without), and having multiple lines only nudges churn up (28.6% vs 25.0%).

The fiber result deserves a closer look, so let us check the obvious explanation - price.

Insight. Fiber customers pay $91.50 a month on average - roughly $33 more than DSL (\$58.10) and four times the no-internet group ($21.08) - while having no more tenure to show for it. Combined with the MonthlyCharges

It is also a large problem, not a niche one: fiber customers make up 69.4% of everyone who churned.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 8))
for ax, col in zip(axes.flat, addons):
    churn_by_category(col, data=internet, ax=ax, title=col)

fig.suptitle("Churn rate by add-on service - internet subscribers only (n = 5,517)",
             fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Insights - the add-ons split cleanly into two kinds.

  • Protective add-ons roughly cut churn by two-thirds. Among internet subscribers, customers without OnlineSecurity churn at 41.8% against 14.6% for those who have it; TechSupport is almost identical (41.6% vs 15.2%). OnlineBackup (39.9% vs 21.5%) and DeviceProtection (39.1% vs 22.5%) point the same way but are noticeably weaker.
  • Streaming add-ons do essentially nothing. StreamingTV (33.5% without vs 30.1% with) and StreamingMovies (33.7% vs 29.9%) are nearly flat - spreads of just 3.5 and 3.7 points - the two weakest of the six.

The genuine contrast is therefore between support-type services, which make an account stickier by solving problems and building a support relationship, and entertainment extras, which add to the bill without creating any attachment. For retention, security and tech support are real tools; streaming is not one.

Yes 17.98 74.44 1531.80

Insights.

  • Churned customers are new customers. Mean tenure is 18.0 months for churners against 37.6 for those who stay, and the churned histogram is dominated by a huge spike in the first few months. The retained distribution, by contrast, piles up at 72 months.
  • Churned customers pay more. Mean monthly charge is $74.44 vs $61.27. The churned histogram is concentrated in the $70-$100 band - exactly where the fiber bundles sit.
  • TotalCharges is lower for churners ($1,532 vs $2,550), but this is arithmetic, not insight: they paid more per month for far fewer months. It is a consequence of the first two findings rather than a separate one.

The profile of a churner is now quite specific: new, paying a high monthly bill, on a monthly contract, with fiber internet and no support add-ons.

7.6 Churn across the customer lifetime¶

Since tenure is so important, the clearest way to see it is to group customers into tenure bands and plot churn for each.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))

Insight -mote important chart of analysis.

Churn falls monotonically and steeply with tenure:

Tenure band Churn rate Customers
0-12 months 47.4% 2,186
13-24 months 28.7% 1,024
25-48 months 20.4% 1,594
49-60 months 14.4% 832
61-72 months 6.6% 1,407

Nearly half of all first-year customers leave, against 6.6% of those past five years - a 7x difference, and the widest spread of any grouping in this notebook (40.8 points). The first band is also the largest, at 2,186 customers.

Two things follow:

  1. Retention is won or lost in the first 12 months. Once a customer passes roughly the two-year mark they become structurally safe. Money spent on year-one onboarding therefore returns far more than money spent on long-tenure customers.
  2. Survivorship explains part of the curve - the customers still present at 60+ months are, by definition, the ones who never wanted to leave, so the low churn there is partly a definition rather than a finding. But survivorship does not explain the size of the year-one spike, which is a genuine early-life failure.

10. Summary of findings¶

Overall churn rate: 26.5% (1,869 of 7,043 customers).

The drivers, strongest first¶

Rank Driver Finding Spread
1 Tenure First year 47.4%, falling to 6.6% past five years - a 7x gap. 40.8 pts
2 Contract type Monthly 42.7% vs two-year 2.8% - a 15x difference. 55% of customers are on monthly terms. 39.9 pts
3 Internet service Fiber 41.9% vs DSL 19.0% vs no internet 7.4%. Fiber is 69.4% of all churners. 34.5 pts
4 Online security / tech support Absent 41.8% / 41.6% vs present 14.6% / 15.2% (internet subscribers). 27.2 / 26.5 pts
5 Payment method Manual 34.7% vs automatic 16.7% / 15.2%. 19.4 pts
6 Senior citizen 41.7% vs 23.6% - nearly double. 18.1 pts
7 Paperless billing Yes 33.6% vs no 16.3% - a marker of risk, not a cause. 17.2 pts
8 Household No dependents 31.3% vs 15.5%; no partner 33.0% vs 19.7%. 15.8 / 13.3 pts
9 Monthly charges Churners pay $74.44 vs $61.27 on average. -

What does not predict churn¶

Gender (0.8 pts), phone service (1.8 pts), multiple lines (3.6 pts), and - once no-internet customers are correctly excluded - both streaming add-ons (3.5 and 3.7 pts). Flat enough to ignore. Worth stating explicitly, because gender in particular is a common thing to chart and it earns no place in a retention strategy.

The profile of a customer about to leave¶

New (under 12 months), on a monthly contract, with fiber optic internet, paying a high monthly bill, paying manually, with no online security or tech support, living alone. In the worst combination measured - monthly contract with fiber - 54.6% churn.

Interpretation, honestly stated¶

The three headline drivers are not fully independent. Monthly contracts, short tenure, and manual payment describe overlapping populations, and part of the contract effect is selection (customers who intended to stay were willing to sign a long contract) rather than pure causation (the contract locking them in). Both mechanisms are real and both are commercially useful, but the honest reading is that the 15x contract gap is an upper bound on what contract migration alone could achieve.

Confirming the size of the causal share would need a controlled test rather than more analysis of this dataset.

11. Business recommendations¶

  1. Move monthly customers onto annual contracts. The largest single opportunity: 3,875 customers on 42.7% churn, against 2.8% on two-year terms. Even a modest discount for committing a year is cheap against losing 4 in 10 of them. Target monthly-contract fiber customers first - that cell alone runs at 54.6%.
  2. Build a serious first-year onboarding programme. Nearly half of first-year customers leave. Proactive check-ins at months 1, 3 and 6 attack churn where it actually happens, and every customer carried past ~24 months becomes structurally safe.
  3. Investigate fiber pricing and quality. Fiber customers pay $91.50 a month - $33 more than DSL - churn at 41.9%, and account for 69% of all churn. Whether the issue is price, reliability or unmet expectations cannot be settled from this dataset, but it is the single most valuable question to answer next, and it needs service-quality and complaint data to answer properly.
  4. Push automatic payment enrolment. Manual payers churn at 34.7% against roughly 16% for automatic. A small enrolment incentive is one of the cheapest interventions available, and it removes a recurring "should I keep paying for this?" moment.
  5. Bundle security and tech support as retention tools, not upsells. Among internet subscribers they cut churn from roughly 42% to 15% - about two-thirds. Offering them free to at-risk customers is very likely cheaper than losing the account. Do not use streaming add-ons this way: once measured correctly they barely move churn at all (3-4 points), so they add to the bill without making the account any stickier.
  6. Support the fragile segments directly. Senior citizens (41.7%) and single-person households are structurally more likely to leave and would benefit from simpler plans and a clearer support path.
  7. Stop segmenting on gender. It has no relationship with churn whatsoever.

Suggested next steps¶

  • Combine drivers into a simple risk score (contract + tenure + internet type + payment method) to produce a ranked at-risk list for the retention team.
  • Run a controlled test on contract migration to separate selection from causation before committing a large discount budget.
  • Bring in data this dataset does not contain - complaint history, outage records, network quality, and competitor pricing by area - which is most likely where the real explanation for the fiber result lives.
